column3: Repeats the focus's conditional question: if it is from God yet you reject it, wrongdoing leaves no guidance.
A fire-dwellers' plea for relief supplies a consequence scene for the focus's rejected message.
Seeking to lead others astray while only harming oneself parallels the focus's misguidance judgment.
Its challenge asks who can shield disbelievers from painful punishment, extending the consequence of rejection.
The same-surah return of Hour-knowledge to God gives nearby eschatological context but not the schism.
Explicitly calls the wrongdoers' condition a distant schism, directly matching the focus's final diagnosis.
The rhetorical question about another god and divine provision broadly counters rejection but lacks the focus's schism.
Names a community led astray after Moses, but does not address rejecting a divine message.
Disbelievers call the summoned day difficult, supplying only a broad judgment consequence.
Contrasts self-incurred straying with guidance received through revelation, clarifying the focus's source-and-rejection logic.
Nearby identification of afterlife disbelievers gives local context without developing distant opposition.
Rejecting the truth-bearing Book produces explicit distant schism, closely matching both the cause and diagnosis.
The challenge over lost hearing, sight, and hearts shows refusal despite signs, but not the focus's schism.
It explicitly places criminals in misguidance, though the accompanying fire imagery differs from distant schism.
Opposition to God and His messenger directly embodies the hostile separation named in the focus.
A clear proof and mercy from the Lord that people resist parallels rejection of a divine source.
The same-surah skeptic doubts the Hour and claims privilege after mercy, a local instance of rejection.
Idols leading many astray relates to misguidance, but not specifically to rejecting revelation.
Its formula names the most astray as those invoking others besides God, closely paralleling the focus's verdict.
Wandering in the land gives a concrete image of misguidance, though in a distinct disciplinary setting.
The earth being split for growth does not clarify rejection, misguidance, or schism.
The companion describes the condemned person as in distant misguidance, an exact counterpart to the focus's distant schism.
The same surah records explicit disbelief in what the messengers were sent with, directly setting up 41:52.
Plotting before God does not materially develop the rejection-and-schism judgment.
Turning away from shared faith is explicitly called schism, supplying a close formulation of the focus's opposition.
Those in the Fire admit messengers brought proofs; their futile prayer is called misguidance, closely linking rejection and outcome.
Calling on another god without proof and facing account at the Lord gives a broad parallel to culpable disbelief.
It warns of the day made severe by disbelief, but does not add the focus's source or schism.
The same-surah disbelievers in punishment identify those who led them astray, developing the focus's consequence context.
The promised removal of the righteous from the Fire is a contrast, not a direct account of rejection or schism.
Following desire without guidance from God is called the utmost misguidance, directly illuminating the focus's rhetorical verdict.
Rejecting a messenger as merely human and naming the result misguidance parallels the focus's refusal pattern.
Regarding the promised event as distant contrasts with the focus's distant schism but adds little else.
It explicitly joins ingratitude or disbelief to severe punishment, a broad consequence parallel.
The same-surah summons to the one God and straightness provides the positive alternative to the focus's distant schism.
Opposing God and His messenger and receiving severe punishment closely characterizes the hostile separation in the focus.
A warning of renewed destruction for disbelief gives consequence context but not the focus's main relation.
Briefly states their rejection of it and coming knowledge, echoing the focus's rejected divine source.
Recompense for one who was rejected is a distinct Noah setting and only loosely parallels rejection.
Marital discord uses the same schism term in an unrelated social setting.
The same surah explicitly identifies those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it comes to them, directly anticipating the focus.
A family's mistaken charge of evident error is not the focus's rejection of divine revelation.
They previously rejected it and now speak from a distant place, closely combining the focus's rejection and distance motifs.
Aaron's warning after the calf trial offers guidance rejected by a community, though without the distant-schism language.
The devil is called a manifest misleader in a narrative conflict, a distant connection only.
Creation by God's command does not clarify rejecting a divine message or being in schism.
The same-surah return to God and bodily testimony provide nearby accountability context for the focus's warning.
Schism with the prophet is warned to bring prior peoples' punishment, closely pairing opposition and consequence.
Rejecting God when He alone is invoked and believing with association directly explains the disbelief challenged in the focus.
Guiding the Prophet after being unaware is a different sense and setting of being lost.
Following desire without knowledge leaves no guide, a general explanation of the focus's misguidance.
Disbelief after faith and punishment for criminality form a broad rejection-and-consequence parallel.
The same-surah sign of reviving the dead grounds the divine power behind the focus's eschatological warning.
Disputing the Hour is explicitly called distant misguidance, strongly paralleling the focus's distant schism.
Turning away after being reminded of the Lord's signs and receiving retribution closely parallels culpable rejection.
Fruit and its sheaths do not clarify the focus's rejection or distant schism.
The condemned admit denying the warner and denying divine sending, directly paralleling rejection of a divine source.
Doubt or faith in the Hereafter gives only a broad epistemic background to the focus.
The same-surah false objects of invocation vanish and no escape remains, a direct consequence context for the focus's rejection.
On the Day of Resurrection, partners tied to schism fail and disbelievers are disgraced, closely matching hostile separation.
Disbelief and blocking God's way cause deeds to go astray, extending the focus's misguidance outcome.
The threat of a burdensome ascent does not clarify the focus's source, rejection, or schism.
Pharaoh led his people astray rather than guided them, a general instance of the focus's misguidance.
For one left astray no path can be found, sharpening the focus's verdict but in a different context.
The same-surah witness scene gives accountability context without the focus's rejection or distant division.
God knows who has strayed from His way and who is guided, broadly framing the focus's question.
The same surah contrasts the Quran as guidance with deafness, blindness, and being called from a distant place for disbelievers.
Stubborn opposition to divine signs relates to refusal but adds little to the focus's articulated judgment.
Knowledge belonging to God and clear warning give general revelation context, not the focus's schism.
Those in misguidance eventually see the promised punishment and their worse station, extending the focus's consequence horizon.
The same-surah creation account does not clarify rejection, misguidance, or schism.
Opposing the messenger after guidance and following another path ends in Hell, closely explaining the focus's distant separation.
Rules for written debt and testimony do not materially illuminate the focus.
Grain, fragrant plants, and husks do not clarify the focus's rejection or schism.
Punishment from God is mentioned, but the verse does not develop rejection of revelation or misguidance.
Disbelief and blocking God's path culminate in the Fire, a broad consequence parallel to the focus.
Addressing disbelievers supplies only the focus's audience category without its argument or outcome.
A later confession of manifest misguidance gives a consequence-side parallel, though not distant schism.
Wrongdoers fearing what they earned gives judgment context but not the focus's rejection mechanism.
Divergent striving is a general contrast to straight guidance, without the focus's divine-source claim.
Disbelievers receiving recompense for deeds provides only a broad consequence frame.
The rhetorical dependence on God for water broadly counters denial but lacks the focus's misguidance relation.
Personal guidance is not harmed by another's straying and all return to God, a broad counterpart to the focus.
An impending punishment challenge supplies general warning context only.
False worship followed by punishment gives a limited rejection-and-consequence parallel.
The challenge to bring a more guiding Book from God directly engages the focus's claim of a divine source and guidance.
Despair is associated with disbelief, but the verse does not address rejecting revelation or distant schism.
A prophet's proof and mercy from God that opponents reject broadly parallels the focus's conditional challenge.
Calling alternative worship manifest misguidance parallels the focus's verdict, though without its distant-schism wording.
The rhetorical question about another god and divine provision broadly counters disbelief but lacks the focus's schism.
Demanding a different revelation and the prophet's refusal to alter what is revealed directly illustrate rejecting a divine message.
God's knowledge of those who stray from His path and those guided directly frames the focus's misguidance question.
Failure to answer the Quranic challenge establishes its descent by God's knowledge, closely matching the focus's source claim.
Reward with the Lord contrasts with distant schism but does not develop the focus's rejection.
Etiquette and household boundaries do not materially illuminate the focus.
Iblis's pride and disbelief illustrate rejection of a divine command, though not the focus's distant schism.
Exclusive worship of God supplies the positive alternative to the rejection described in the focus.
Blindness in this world becoming greater loss of the way in the Hereafter strongly extends the focus's misguidance trajectory.
Invoking what harms more than benefits gives a concrete form of the misguided devotion contrasted by the focus.
Associating partners with God is explicitly called far misguidance, closely matching the focus's distant schism after rejection.
Disbelief in God, His angels, Books, messengers, and the Last Day is explicitly called going far astray, directly joining rejected revelation to distance.
Those who disbelieve and hinder God's path are explicitly said to have gone far astray, a close consequence pattern for the focus.
Those who prefer worldly life, hinder God's path, and seek its crookedness are explicitly placed in far error.
Disbelievers in the Hereafter are placed in punishment and far error, extending the focus's judgment horizon.
Turning to false judgment rather than divine direction is paired with Satan's aim of leading people far astray.
It condemns denying the truth when it comes, directly paralleling the focus's challenge about rejecting what is from God.
Denying the truth upon its arrival is named among the gravest wrongs, a direct parallel to the focus's rejection premise.
Denying God's signs is joined to the gravest wrongdoing, strongly supporting the focus's condemnation of refusal.
Fabricating against God or denying His signs is called the height of wrongdoing, closely related to the focus's verdict.
The question over who is more unjust than one who lies about God or denies His signs parallels the focus's rhetorical condemnation.
Those who fabricate against God are identified as wrongdoers before their Lord, supplying a direct truth-rejection counterpart.
Inventing lies about God while called to submission joins false attribution and refusal of the divine call.
They disbelieve in what God sent beyond their inherited scripture even though it confirms truth, closely matching the focus's conditional accusation.
A group casts aside God's Book after a confirming messenger arrives, an enactment of the refusal described in the focus.
People of the Book are challenged over disbelieving in God's signs while witnessing them, a concise parallel to culpable rejection.
Discriminating among God and His messengers defines a direct form of disbelief in revealed authority.
Turning away after being reminded of the Lord's signs closely parallels the focus's rejection of a divine communication.
Turning away from divine remembrance produces a constricted life and later accountability, extending the consequence of refusal.
The messenger's complaint that his people abandoned the Quran directly names a communal form of rejecting revelation.
Revelation by God's command is made a light through which He guides, supplying the positive source-and-guidance counterpart to the focus.
When the truth comes, opponents call it magic and reject it, directly illustrating the refusal hypothesized in the focus.
After God's signs are recited in truth, the verse asks what discourse they can believe in, sharpening the focus's challenge to disbelief.
People reject messengers who bring clear proofs and turn away, a direct narrative of the focus's rejection premise.
Those who deny the Book and what was sent with messengers are warned of a coming consequence, closely related to the focus's source claim.
Calling the revealed message human speech directly exemplifies denying a communication that comes from God.
